mercy_translation.text:
Many kings and tyrants have existed on earth before him; many wise men and magicians are recorded among the Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Indians. Which of these, I do not say after death but even while still alive, was ever able to exert such power as to fill the whole earth with his teaching and turn so great a multitude away from the superstition of idols as our Savior has transferred from idols to himself?

The philosophers of the Greeks wrote many things with persuasive and artful speech. Yet what have they displayed equal to the cross of Christ? Their arguments retained some plausibility until their deaths; but even the influence they seemed to possess while alive was exercised in rivalry with one another, contending and composing arguments against each other.

But the Word of God—most astonishingly—teaching through simpler language, overshadowed the great sophists. He abolished their teachings, drew everyone toward himself, and filled his own churches. And what is remarkable is that, by descending to death as a human being, he abolished the grand discourse of the wise concerning idols.

Whose death ever drove away demons? Or whose death did demons ever fear as they fear Christ's? Wherever the Savior's name is named, every demon is driven away. And who has so removed the passions of the soul from human beings that the sexually immoral become self-controlled, murderers no longer hold the sword, and those formerly held by cowardice become courageous?

In general, who persuaded peoples called barbarian and the nations in various regions to lay aside frenzy and think thoughts of peace except faith in Christ and the sign of the cross? Who else so convinced human beings concerning immortality as did the cross of Christ and the resurrection of his body?

Although the Greeks invented all kinds of false stories, they were not able to fabricate a resurrection for their idols. They did not even seriously conceive that a body might exist again after death. In this especially one may commend them, for by thinking in this way they exposed the weakness of their own idolatry and conceded the possibility to Christ, so that from this too he might be known by all as the Son of God.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The chapter contrasts Christian claims about resurrection and moral transformation with Greek philosophical and religious traditions.
The language about 'barbarian' peoples is historical terminology from Athanasius' world and should not be adopted as a modern value judgment.
